content.text: How can electricity travel hundreds of kilometres from power stations to our homes without losing most of its energy? The answer involves transformers—devices that change AC voltage up or down. Transformers are essential to our power grid and are found in countless devices from phone chargers to substations.

A transformer changes AC voltage using two coils wound on a shared iron core. The ratio of turns on the primary and secondary coils determines whether the voltage is stepped up or stepped down. Transformers only work with AC because a changing current is needed to produce a changing magnetic field.
changes the voltage of an alternating current (AC) supply.

content.text: Example: A 10:1 step-down transformer converts 230 V to 23 V.
If voltage goes UP, current goes DOWN (and vice versa).
Step-up transformer: higher voltage, lower current
Step-down transformer: lower voltage, higher current

When using the transformer equation Vp/Vs = np/ns, always check which coil is primary and which is secondary. The primary is connected to the input (AC supply) and the secondary is connected to the output (load). A common exam error is to swap the two.

For an ideal transformer, power in equals power out (VpIp = VsIs). If voltage goes up, current must come down by the same factor. This is why the National Grid uses high voltage for transmission -- it reduces the current and therefore reduces energy lost as heat in the cables (P = I squared R).

DC produces a constant current, which creates a constant magnetic field in the core. A constant field means zero rate of change of flux through the secondary coil. With no changing flux, no voltage is induced in the secondary — so the transformer does not work.
Ps = Vs x Is = 12 x 2 = 24 W
At 100% efficiency: VpIp = VsIs, so Ip = VsIs / Vp = 24 / 240 = 0.1 A

Resistance heating in the coils (I²R losses) — reduced by using thick, low-resistance copper wire. Eddy currents induced in the iron core cause heating — reduced by laminating the core (thin insulated sheets interrupt the eddy current paths).

Power transmitted P = IV. For the same power, increasing voltage reduces current. Power lost in cables = I²R, so reducing the current dramatically reduces energy wasted as heat in the cables. Doubling the voltage halves the current and quarters the losses.
Ps = efficiency x Pp = 0.95 x 500 = 475 W
